paragraphs.heading: A war without direct fighting
paragraphs.text: The Cold War was a long rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies: the capitalist Western Bloc against the communist Eastern Bloc. It began after the Second World War and ended when the Soviet Union broke up in 1991. It is called cold because the two superpowers never fought each other directly. Instead, each backed opposite sides in regional conflicts called proxy wars.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name came from
paragraphs.text: Orwell wrote in The Observer in March 1946 that Russia had started a cold war against Britain and its empire. The first use of the term for the US–Soviet standoff came in an April 1947 speech by Bernard Baruch, an adviser to Democratic presidents, written by the journalist Herbert Bayard Swope. The columnist Walter Lippmann spread the term with his book The Cold War. Asked where it came from, Lippmann traced it to a French phrase of the 1930s, la guerre froide.

paragraphs.heading: Allies become rivals
paragraphs.text: The US and the Soviet Union had been allies in the Second World War. By 1949, though, the Soviets had installed satellite governments in the lands they occupied in Eastern Europe and in North Korea, dividing Europe and Germany along an Iron Curtain. That same year the Soviet Union tested its first nuclear weapon and allied with the newly founded People's Republic of China. The US, for its part, declared the Truman Doctrine of containing communism in 1947, launched the Marshall Plan for Western Europe's recovery in 1948, and founded the NATO alliance in 1949, which the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact matched in 1955.

paragraphs.heading: Flashpoints
paragraphs.text: Early clashes included the Berlin Blockade of 1948 to 1949 and the Korean War, fought from 1950 to 1953 and ending in a stalemate. In 1962 the Cuban Missile Crisis began after the US placed missiles in Europe and the Soviets placed missiles in Cuba. It is widely seen as the moment the Cold War came nearest to nuclear war. The Vietnam War, from 1955 to 1975, was another major proxy war and ended in victory for North Vietnam. In Europe the Soviets tightened their grip by crushing the Hungarian Revolution in 1956 and through the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968.

paragraphs.heading: A struggle across the globe
paragraphs.text: As nearly all the colonies gained independence, many of them became Third World battlefields of the Cold War. Both powers offered economic aid to try to win the loyalty of countries that had not taken a side. The US supported anti-communist and right-wing dictatorships and uprisings. The Soviets funded left-wing parties, wars of independence and dictatorships.

paragraphs.heading: Thaw, chill and collapse
paragraphs.text: The Soviet Union and China fell out too: relations between them had broken down by 1961, and a border conflict in 1969 brought them to the edge of war. In 1972 the US opened contacts with China, and the US and the Soviet Union signed treaties limiting their nuclear weapons during a period known as détente. Tensions rose again in 1979, when governments allied to the US fell in Iran and Nicaragua and the Soviet–Afghan War broke out. Mikhail Gorbachev took over the Soviet Union in 1985 and widened political freedoms, which helped bring about the Eastern Bloc revolutions of 1989 and the Soviet collapse of 1991 that ended the Cold War.
